Fulnek
fool'nek
n. (Moravian town; Comenius's first parish, burned in 1621 with his library)
From German Fulnek, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a Slavic stream name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Fulnek was John Amos Comenius's first and only settled parish. He was ordained to it in 1618, a young Brethren minister with a school attached and a scheme of educational reform already forming; in 1621, after the Bohemian defeat at the White Mountain, Spanish troops took the town, burned it, and destroyed his house with his library and his manuscripts in it. His wife and both children died in the plague and persecution that followed, and he spent the remaining forty-nine years of his life in exile, writing the books that made him the father of modern pedagogy and the last bishop of a church that no longer had a country. The dictionary records Fulnek because Comenius's losses were total and his output was enormous, which is only explicable on one principle. “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines loss as privation, as the loss of property or of health; substance as goods, estate, that which is real and permanent; and to spoil as to plunder or strip by violence.

expand to see more

LOSS, n. Privation; as the loss of property; the loss of health.

SUBSTANCE, n. Goods; estate; means of living; that which is real and permanent.

SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to take by force from an enemy.

TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve.

Key Scripture

Job 1:21 — "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Php 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,"

Heb 10:34 — "For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance."

Mat 6:20 — "But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:"

Modern Corruption

Comenius's parish from 1618, burned in 1621 with his library; forty-nine years of exile followed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern expectation that catastrophic loss ends a man's usefulness, which is sometimes true and was not true here. Comenius lost house, books, wife, children and country in four years and wrote for half a century afterwards.

The principle to recover is that an enduring substance in heaven makes the loss of everything here survivable without pretending it is small. Job's words are the model, and they are spoken in grief: “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). Paul reckons the exchange deliberately: “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8). The Hebrews are commended for the ground of their composure: they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34). And the Lord's own direction follows: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zemia (G2209), loss or damage; Greek huparxis (G5223), substance or possession.

Hebrew barak (H1288) — to bless, to speak well of; Job 1:21.

Greek zemia (G2209) — loss, damage, forfeiture; Philippians 3:8.

Greek huperecho (G5242) — to surpass, to be superior; Philippians 3:8.

Greek harpage (G724) — plundering, a seizing of goods; Hebrews 10:34.

Greek huparxis (G5223) — substance, goods, possession; Hebrews 10:34.

Usage

"“the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away” (Job 1:21) — the town burned in 1621."

"“I count all things but loss” (Php 3:8) — his library and manuscripts destroyed with his house."

"“ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34) — and forty-nine years of writing in exile."
